Predictive Maintenance Using Machine Learning in Industrial IoT¶

Project Title: Predictive Maintenance Using Machine Learning in Industrial IoT
Dataset: AI4I 2020 Predictive Maintenance Dataset (UCI Machine Learning Repository)
Dataset Source: https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/601/ai4i+2020+predictive+maintenance+dataset
Approach: Systematic — Post-positivist, Deductive, Cross-sectional Computational
Classifiers: Random Forest, XGBoost, Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)
Techniques: SMOTE (class imbalance), SHAP (explainability), Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation
Evaluation Metrics: Macro-averaged F1-score, ROC-AUC (One-vs-Rest), Precision, Recall

Project Pipeline Overview¶

The notebook follows a sequential four-phase pipeline:

  1. Data Ingestion, Cleaning, and Quality Check
  2. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Feature Engineering
  3. Preprocessing, SMOTE, and Model Training
  4. Evaluation, Comparative Analysis, and SHAP Explainability

2. Data Loading¶

The AI4I 2020 Predictive Maintenance Dataset contains 10,000 synthetic but physically realistic observations of a CNC milling machine. It includes 14 attributes across sensor readings and five binary fault mode labels (Matzka, 2020).

3. Data Cleaning and Quality Check¶

This section performs a systematic quality assessment covering: missing values, duplicate records, data type validation, and identifier column removal. These steps ensure that the dataset entering the modelling pipeline is structurally sound and free from artefacts that could compromise classifier performance (Zonta et al., 2020).

3.1 Missing Value Analysis¶

In [6]:
# Check for missing values across all columns
missing = df.isnull().sum()
missing_pct = (missing / len(df) * 100).round(2)
missing_df = pd.DataFrame({'Missing Count': missing, 'Missing Percentage': missing_pct})
missing_df = missing_df[missing_df['Missing Count'] > 0]

if missing_df.empty:
    print("No missing values detected in the dataset.")
else:
    print("Missing values found:")
    print(missing_df)

3.5 Outlier Detection — Interquartile Range Method¶

In [10]:
# IQR-based outlier detection on continuous sensor features
sensor_features = [
    'Air temperature [K]', 'Process temperature [K]',
    'Rotational speed [rpm]', 'Torque [Nm]', 'Tool wear [min]'
]

print("Outlier summary per sensor feature (IQR method):")
print(f"{'Feature':<35} {'Q1':>8} {'Q3':>8} {'IQR':>8} {'Lower':>10} {'Upper':>10} {'Outliers':>10}")
print("-" * 95)

outlier_summary = {}
for col in sensor_features:
    Q1 = df[col].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = df[col].quantile(0.75)
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    lower = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
    upper = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
    n_out = ((df[col] < lower) | (df[col] > upper)).sum()
    outlier_summary[col] = n_out
    print(f"{col:<35} {Q1:>8.2f} {Q3:>8.2f} {IQR:>8.2f} {lower:>10.2f} {upper:>10.2f} {n_out:>10}")

print()
print("Note: Outliers are retained as they may represent genuine fault-inducing conditions.")

5. Feature Engineering¶

Feature engineering derives physically meaningful variables from raw sensor readings to enhance classifier discriminative power. Four derived features are created based on the thermodynamic and mechanical relationships inherent in the CNC milling process (Achouch et al., 2023).

5.1 Target Variable Construction¶

In [23]:
# Construct a multi-class target variable from the five binary fault labels
# Priority order: TWF > HDF > PWF > OSF > RNF > No failure (0)
# Rationale: This matches the typical maintenance severity ordering in the literature (Matzka, 2020)

fault_priority = ['TWF', 'HDF', 'PWF', 'OSF', 'RNF']
fault_class_map = {'No Failure': 0, 'TWF': 1, 'HDF': 2, 'PWF': 3, 'OSF': 4, 'RNF': 5}

def assign_fault_class(row):
    for fault in fault_priority:
        if row[fault] == 1:
            return fault_class_map[fault]
    return 0  # No failure

df['Fault_Class'] = df.apply(assign_fault_class, axis=1)

class_dist = df['Fault_Class'].value_counts().sort_index()
label_names = {0: 'No Failure', 1: 'TWF', 2: 'HDF', 3: 'PWF', 4: 'OSF', 5: 'RNF'}

print("Multi-class Target Variable Distribution:")
print(f"{'Class':>6}  {'Label':<15} {'Count':>8} {'Percentage':>12}")
print("-" * 45)
for cls, count in class_dist.items():
    pct = count / len(df) * 100
    print(f"{cls:>6}  {label_names[cls]:<15} {count:>8,} {pct:>11.2f}%")
print(f"Total records: {len(df):,}")

5.2 Derived Features¶

In [24]:
# Feature 1 — Temperature Difference (Process - Air)
# Physical rationale: The temperature differential between process and ambient indicates
# heat dissipation efficiency. A smaller-than-expected difference signals HDF risk.
df['Temp_Difference_K'] = df['Process temperature [K]'] - df['Air temperature [K]']

# Feature 2 — Mechanical Power (Torque x Angular Velocity)
# Physical rationale: Power = Torque × (2π/60 × RPM) reflects actual mechanical load.
# Excessive power indicates PWF risk.
df['Power_W'] = df['Torque [Nm]'] * (2 * np.pi / 60) * df['Rotational speed [rpm]']

# Feature 3 — Tool Wear Rate (Tool Wear / Rotational Speed)
# Physical rationale: Higher tool wear at lower speeds indicates aggressive cutting conditions.
# Elevated values correlate with TWF and OSF risk.
df['Tool_Wear_Rate'] = df['Tool wear [min]'] / (df['Rotational speed [rpm]'] + 1e-6)

# Feature 4 — Torque-Speed Ratio
# Physical rationale: Captures mechanical operating regime; extreme ratios indicate stress.
df['Torque_Speed_Ratio'] = df['Torque [Nm]'] / (df['Rotational speed [rpm]'] + 1e-6)

print("Derived features created:")
print(f"  Temp_Difference_K    — Thermal differential (Process - Air)")
print(f"  Power_W              — Mechanical power in Watts (Torque x Angular velocity)")
print(f"  Tool_Wear_Rate       — Tool wear per unit rotational speed")
print(f"  Torque_Speed_Ratio   — Ratio of torque to rotational speed")
print()
print("Statistics for derived features:")
derived = ['Temp_Difference_K', 'Power_W', 'Tool_Wear_Rate', 'Torque_Speed_Ratio']
print(df[derived].describe().round(4))

Derived features created:
  Temp_Difference_K    — Thermal differential (Process - Air)
  Power_W              — Mechanical power in Watts (Torque x Angular velocity)
  Tool_Wear_Rate       — Tool wear per unit rotational speed
  Torque_Speed_Ratio   — Ratio of torque to rotational speed

6. Data Preprocessing¶

Preprocessing converts the cleaned and engineered dataset into a format suitable for ML training. Steps include: feature matrix construction, stratified train-test splitting, and z-score normalisation. SMOTE is applied inside the training fold only to prevent data leakage into the test set (Zonta et al., 2020; Matzka, 2020).

6.1 Feature Matrix and Target Vector Construction¶

In [27]:

y = df[target_col].copy()

print(f"Target vector y shape:  {y.shape}")

    print(f"  Class {cls} ({label_names[cls]:<12}): {count:>6,}  ({count/len(y)*100:.2f}%)")

# Fit StandardScaler on training data only; transform both train and test sets
# This prevents test set statistics from influencing the scaling parameters.

X_test_scaled  = scaler.transform(X_test)

X_test_scaled  = pd.DataFrame(X_test_scaled,  columns=feature_cols)

7. Model Training — Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation with Grid Search¶

Three classifiers are trained: Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). Each classifier undergoes hyperparameter optimisation via grid search with stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Models are evaluated on the held-out test set which retains the original imbalanced distribution, ensuring that performance metrics reflect real-world conditions (Fink et al., 2020; Serradilla et al., 2022).

7.1 Cross-Validation Configuration¶

7.3 XGBoost Classifier¶

In [42]:
import pandas as pd
# XGBoost — Grid Search Hyperparameter Optimisation
print("Training XGBoost with Grid Search...")
print()

# Compute class weights for XGBoost
from collections import Counter
class_counts = Counter(y_train_smote)
n_total = len(y_train_smote)
n_classes = len(class_counts)

# Sanitize feature names for XGBoost
# XGBoost does not allow certain characters like [, ], < in feature names.
# This operation modifies X_train_smote and X_test_scaled in place for subsequent XGBoost usage.
def sanitize_feature_names(df):
    new_columns = []
    for col in df.columns:
        # Replace problematic characters with underscores
        new_col = col.replace('[', '_').replace(']', '_').replace('<', '_').replace('>', '_').strip()
        new_columns.append(new_col)
    df.columns = new_columns
    return df

X_train_smote = sanitize_feature_names(X_train_smote)
X_test_scaled = sanitize_feature_names(X_test_scaled)

# Ensure the global feature_cols list is also updated to reflect the new names.
# This is crucial for SHAP and other parts that use feature_cols to match the model's feature names.
sanitized_feature_cols = []
for col in feature_cols:
    new_col = col.replace('[', '_').replace(']', '_').replace('<', '_').replace('>', '_').strip()
    sanitized_feature_cols.append(new_col)
feature_cols = sanitized_feature_cols

xgb_param_grid = {
    'learning_rate':  [0.01, 0.1],
    'n_estimators':   [100, 300],
    'max_depth':      [3, 6],
    'subsample':      [0.8, 1.0],
    'colsample_bytree': [0.8, 1.0]
}

xgb_base = XGBClassifier(
    objective='multi:softprob',
    num_class=len(classes_present),
    eval_metric='mlogloss',
    use_label_encoder=False,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbosity=0
)

xgb_grid = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=xgb_base,
    param_grid=xgb_param_grid,
    cv=cv,
    scoring='f1_macro',
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=0,
    refit=True
)

xgb_grid.fit(X_train_smote, y_train_smote)

print(f"Best hyperparameters (XGBoost):")
for param, val in xgb_grid.best_params_.items():
    print(f"  {param}: {val}")
print(f" Best cross-validation macro F1-score: {xgb_grid.best_score_:.4f}")

xgb_best = xgb_grid.best_estimator_
print(" XGBoost training complete.")

8. Model Evaluation and Comparative Analysis¶

This section provides a complete evaluation suite covering: confusion matrices for all three classifiers, multi-class ROC-AUC curves, and a consolidated comparative performance table. Macro-averaged metrics are used throughout, as they treat all fault classes equally regardless of their frequency — the appropriate choice under class imbalance (Lundberg et al., 2020).

8.1 Confusion Matrices¶

In [46]:
# Confusion matrices for all three classifiers
class_labels_short = [label_names[c] for c in classes_present]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

preds_list  = [rf_pred, xgb_pred, mlp_pred]
titles_list = ['Random Forest', 'XGBoost', 'MLP']

for i, (pred, title) in enumerate(zip(preds_list, titles_list)):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, pred, labels=classes_present)
    disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm,
                                   display_labels=class_labels_short)
    disp.plot(ax=axes[i], colorbar=False, cmap='Blues')
    axes[i].set_title(f'Figure 9{chr(97+i)}: {title}', fontweight='bold', fontsize=11)
    axes[i].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)
    axes[i].set_xlabel('Predicted Label')
    axes[i].set_ylabel('True Label')

9. SHAP Explainability Analysis¶

SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) TreeExplainer is applied to the best-performing tree-based classifiers (Random Forest and XGBoost). SHAP values provide a theoretically grounded mechanism for distributing feature contributions uniformly across model outputs, enabling both local (instance-level) and global (model-level) interpretability (Lundberg et al., 2020).

For MLP, SHAP KernelExplainer is used with a background summary sample due to the absence of tree structure. A subsample of 1,000 records is used for efficiency, consistent with the risk mitigation strategy defined in Section 3.3 (R03).

9.1 SHAP — Random Forest¶

In [51]:
# SHAP TreeExplainer for Random Forest
print("Computing SHAP values for Random Forest...")

# Subsample for efficiency (Risk R03 mitigation)
sample_idx = np.random.RandomState(42).choice(len(X_test_scaled), size=min(1000, len(X_test_scaled)), replace=False)
X_shap_sample = X_test_scaled.iloc[sample_idx].values

rf_explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(rf_best)
rf_shap_values = rf_explainer.shap_values(X_shap_sample)

print(f"SHAP values computed for {X_shap_sample.shape[0]} test samples.")
print(f"SHAP output shape: {np.array(rf_shap_values).shape}  (classes x samples x features)")

In [54]:
# RF SHAP — Global Bar Plot (mean absolute SHAP across all classes)
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

shap.initjs()

# Average SHAP importance across all fault classes
# rf_shap_values has shape (num_samples, num_features, num_classes)
# First, take absolute values: (num_samples, num_features, num_classes)
# Second, average across classes (axis=2): (num_samples, num_features)
# Third, average across samples (axis=0): (num_features,)
rf_mean_shap_per_feature = np.mean(np.abs(rf_shap_values), axis=(0, 2))

shap_importance_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Feature': feature_cols,
    'Mean Absolute SHAP': rf_mean_shap_per_feature
}).sort_values('Mean Absolute SHAP', ascending=False)

# Local SHAP explanation — single instance waterfall plot (XGBoost, first failure in test set)
# Find the first misclassified failure in the test set for diagnostic insight

# SHAP TreeExplainer for XGBoost (Added to ensure xgb_explainer is defined)
xgb_explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(xgb_best)

failure_indices = np.where(y_test.values != 0)[0]
if len(failure_indices) > 0:
    instance_idx = failure_indices[0]
    instance_sample = X_test_scaled.iloc[instance_idx:instance_idx+1]

    xgb_instance_shap = xgb_explainer.shap_values(instance_sample)

    # Predicted class
    pred_class = xgb_best.predict(instance_sample)[0]
    true_class = y_test.values[instance_idx]
    class_idx_for_waterfall = list(classes_present).index(pred_class)

    print(f"Instance selected: Test set index {instance_idx}")
    print(f"True class:        {true_class} ({label_names[true_class]})"
)
    print(f"Predicted class:   {pred_class} ({label_names[pred_class]})"
)
    print()
    print("SHAP contributions for predicted class:")
    # xgb_instance_shap is (1, num_features, num_classes)
    # Extract shap values for the predicted class
    contrib_values = xgb_instance_shap[0, :, class_idx_for_waterfall]

    contrib_df = pd.DataFrame({
        'Feature': feature_cols,
        'SHAP Value': contrib_values
    }).sort_values('SHAP Value', key=abs, ascending=False)
    print(contrib_df.to_string(index=False))

    # Waterfall-style bar plot (manual, compatible with all SHAP versions)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
    contrib_df_sorted = contrib_df.sort_values('SHAP Value')
    colors = ['#E53935' if v > 0 else '#1976D2' for v in contrib_df_sorted['SHAP Value']]
    ax.barh(contrib_df_sorted['Feature'], contrib_df_sorted['SHAP Value'],
            color=colors, edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.5)
    ax.axvline(0, color='black', linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel('SHAP Value (contribution to predicted class)')
    ax.set_title(f'Figure 17: XGBoost — Local SHAP Explanation\nTrue: {label_names[true_class]} | Predicted: {label_names[pred_class]}',
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig('fig17_shap_waterfall_local.png', bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
else:
    print("No failure instances found in test set for local explanation.")
